{"id": "22f18087-25d2-4d02-a54f-75a6f8ddf31a", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_VttouutsvK308zp3w02nbl", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How can I troubleshoot high latency on DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters?\",\"context\":\"### Misconfiguration in the DAX client\\n\\nIf you lower the **withMinIdleConnectionSize** parameter, then latency across the DAX cluster is likely to increase. This parameter [sets the minimum number of idling connections](http://dax-sdk.s3-website-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/javadocs/hosted/com/amazon/dax/client/dynamodbv2/ClientConfig.html#setMinIdleConnectionSize-int-) with the DAX cluster. For every request, the client will use an available idle connection. If a connection isn't available, then the client establishes a new one. For example, if the parameter is set to 20, then there is a minimum of 20 idle connections with the DAX cluster.\\n\\nThe client maintains a connection pool. When an application makes an API call to DynamoDB or DAX, the client leases a connection from the connection pool. Then, the client makes the API call and returns the connection to the pool. However, the connection pool has an upper limit. If you make a large number of API calls to DAX at once, then they might exceed the limit of the connection pool. In this case, some requests must wait for other requests to complete before obtaining leases from the connection pool. This results in requests queuing up at the connection pool level. As a result, the application experiences an increase in round-trip latency.\\n\\nTherefore, to decrease periodic traffic spikes in your application, adjust the parameters **setMinIdleConnectionSize**, **getMinIdleConnectionSize**, and **withMinIdleConnectionSize**. These parameters play a key role in the latency of a DAX cluster. Configure them for your API calls so that DAX uses an appropriate number of idling connections without the need to reestablish new connections\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/high-latency-dax-clusters\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"DAX and DynamoDB consistency models\",\"context\":\"## Strongly consistent and transactional reads\\n\\nTo perform a strongly consistent `GetItem`, `BatchGetItem`,\\n`Query`, or `Scan` request, you set\\nthe `ConsistentRead` parameter to true. DAX passes strongly consistent\\nread requests to DynamoDB. When it receives a response from DynamoDB, DAX returns the\\nresults to the client, but it does not cache the results. DAX can't serve strongly\\nconsistent reads by itself because it's not tightly coupled to DynamoDB. For this reason,\\nany subsequent reads from DAX would have to be eventually consistent reads. And any\\nsubsequent strongly consistent reads would have to be passed through to DynamoDB.\\n\\nDAX handles `TransactGetItems` requests the same way it handles strongly\\nconsistent reads. DAX passes all `TransactGetItems` requests to DynamoDB. When\\nit receives a response from DynamoDB, DAX returns the results to the client, but it\\ndoesn't cache the results\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.consistency.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Programming DynamoDB with the AWS SDK for Java 2.x\",\"context\":\"### RetryMode\\n\\nAnother configuration related to the timeout configuration that you should\\nconsider is the `RetryMode` configuration object. This configuration\\nobject contains a collection of retry behaviors.\\n\\nThe SDK for Java 2.x supports the following retry modes:\\n\\n* `legacy` \u2013 The default retry mode if you don't\\n explicitly change it. This retry mode is specific to the Java SDK. It's\\n characterized by up to three retries, or more for services such as DynamoDB,\\n which has up to eight retries.\\n* `standard` \u2013 Named \\\"standard\\\" because it's more\\n consistent with other AWS SDKs. For each retry, this mode waits a random\\n amount of time between 0 ms and an exponentially growing ceiling. This\\n approach, called full jitter, fully randomizes each wait rather than using a\\n fixed delay. For DynamoDB, that ceiling starts from a 25 ms base delay and\\n doubles with each subsequent retry, capped at 20 seconds. This mode performs\\n retries on more detected failure conditions than the `legacy`\\n mode. For DynamoDB, it performs up to nine total max attempts unless you\\n override with the maximum number of attempts.\\n* `adaptive`\\n \u2013\\n Builds on `standard` mode and dynamically limits the rate of\\n AWS requests to maximize success rate. This can occur at the expense of\\n request latency. We don't recommend adaptive retry mode when predictable\\n latency is important.\\n\\nYou can find an expanded definition of these retry modes in the Retry\\nbehavior topic in the *AWS SDKs and Tools Reference Guide*.\\n\\nFor information about upcoming changes to the default retry behavior across all\\nAWS SDKs, see Announcing updated retry behavior for AWS SDKs and Tools on the AWS\\nDeveloper Tools Blog. For the exact details for the SDK for Java 2.x, see the retry behavior\\nupdate (discussion #6984) on the GitHub website\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/ProgrammingWithJava.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs for DynamoDB SDK v3 latency, timeout, DAX, and consistency best practices", "parent_id": "5d2402d4-792a-4d70-b750-2611de042b72"}

{"id": "e94955c3-4ebb-491c-a304-0074d663a130", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_kEUe3ArmIpo9mQSVh1q4mD", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot retry and timeout issues when I use an AWS SDK to invoke a Lambda function?\",\"context\":\"### Change the AWS SDK's settings\\n\\nThe retry count and timeout settings of the AWS SDK must allow enough time for your API call to get a response. To find the right values for each setting, test different configurations and get the following information:\\n\\n* Average time to get a successful connection\\n* Average time that a full API request takes until successfully returned\\n\\nFor more information on changing retry count and timeout settings, see the following AWS SDK client configuration documentation:\\n\\n* [Python (Boto 3)](https://botocore.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/config.html)\\n* [JavaScript/Node.js](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v3/developer-guide/welcome.html)\\n* [Java](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaSDK/latest/javadoc/com/amazonaws/ClientConfiguration.html)\\n* [.NET](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-net/latest/developer-guide/retries-timeouts.html)\\n* [Go](https://aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-go/)\\n\\nThe following example commands change retry count and timeout settings for each runtime.\\n\\n**Note:** Be sure to replace the example values for each setting with the values for your scenario.\\n\\n**Example Python (Boto 3) command to change retry count and timeout settings**\\n\\n```plaintext\\n# max_attempts: retry count / read_timeout: socket timeout / connect_timeout: new connection timeout\\nfrom botocore.session import Session\\nfrom botocore.config import Config\\n\\ns = Session()\\nc = s.create_client('s3', config=Config(connect_timeout=5, read_timeout=60, retries={'max_attempts': 2}))\\n```\\n\\n**Example JavaScript V3 command to change retry count and timeout settings**\\n\\n```plaintext\\nconst { S3Client, ListBucketsCommand } = require(\\\"@aws-sdk/client-s3\\\");\\nconst { NodeHttpHandler } = require(\\\"@smithy/node-http-handler\\\");\\n\\nconst client = new S3Client({\\n requestHandler: new NodeHttpHandler({\\n connectionTimeout: 30000,\\n socketTimeout: 50000\\n }),\\n maxAttempts: 2\\n});\\n```\\n\\n**Example Java V2 command to change retry count and timeout settings**\\n\\n```plaintext\\n// apiCallTimeout: total time for the API call including all retries\\n// apiCallAttemptTimeout: time for a single attempt (retriable)\\n// connectionTimeout: time to establish a new connection (HTTP client)\\nimport software\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/lambda-function-retry-timeout-sdk\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot connection timeout issues in DynamoDB?\",\"context\":\"### Update your SDK HTTP timeout settings\\n\\nUpdate the following HTTP timeout settings:\\n\\n* **ConnectionTimeout:** The default value for **ConnectionTimeout** in AWS Java SDK is 10 seconds. If it takes longer than the default time to establish a TCP and TLS socket, then you might have network issues. To resolve this issue, increase the **ConnectionTimeout** value. Or, review your network stability.\\n* **RequestTimeout:** **RequestTimeout** is the time that it takes for the client to complete a single HTTP request. This time includes from the moment a DynamoDB API call is made until a response is received. Set this timeout to a lower setting than the **ClientExecutionTimeout**.\\n* **ClientExecutionTimeout:** **ClientExecutionTimeout** is the maximum total time allowed for an end-to-end operation, including retries. This setting is turned off by default. If you turn on this option, then set it to a value greater than **RequestTimeout** to manage the maximum wait time for a DynamoDB response.\\n* **SocketTimeout:** **SocketTimeout** defines the maximum time that the HTTP client waits to read data from an established TCP connection. Set this value to an amount lesser than the **RequestTimeout** value. For operations like **BatchWriteItem** and **BatchGetItem**, set **SocketTimeout** to a larger value. This larger value makes sure that records are returned as **UnprocessedItems** if an issue occurs at the service end\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/dynamodb-intermittent-timeout-errors\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Reuse connections with keep-alive in Node.js\",\"context\":\"The AWS SDK for JavaScript V3 API\\nReference Guide describes in detail all the API operations for the AWS SDK for JavaScript\\nversion 3 (V3)\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v3/developer-guide/node-reusing-connections.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS SDK JS v3 docs for NodeHttpHandler socket/connection timeout configuration", "parent_id": "5d2402d4-792a-4d70-b750-2611de042b72"}

{"id": "f6c9a765-763a-4af8-8910-6c48f51d14be", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_Y5pVGbnqDsZIFYLKKO7sOK", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Reuse connections with keep-alive in Node.js\",\"context\":\"# Reuse connections with keep-alive in Node.js\\n\\nThe default Node.js HTTP/HTTPS agent creates a new TCP connection for every new\\nrequest. To avoid the cost of establishing a new connection, the AWS SDK for JavaScript reuses TCP\\nconnections *by default*.\\n\\nFor short-lived operations, such as Amazon DynamoDB queries, the latency overhead of\\nsetting up a TCP connection might be greater than the operation itself.\\nAdditionally, since DynamoDB encryption\\nat rest is integrated with AWS KMS, you may experience latencies from the database having to re-establish\\nnew AWS KMS cache entries for each operation.\\n\\nIf you do not want to reuse TCP connections, you can disable reusing these connections alive with `keepAlive` on a per-service client\\nbasis as shown in the following example for a DynamoDB client.\\n\\n```\\nimport { DynamoDBClient } from \\\"@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb\\\";\\nimport { NodeHttpHandler } from \\\"@smithy/node-http-handler\\\";\\nimport { Agent } from \\\"https\\\";\\n\\nconst dynamodbClient = new DynamoDBClient({\\n requestHandler: new NodeHttpHandler({\\n httpsAgent: new Agent({ keepAlive: false })\\n })\\n});\\n```\\n\\nIf `keepAlive` is enabled, you can also set the initial delay for TCP\\nKeep-Alive packets with `keepAliveMsecs`, which by default is 1000 ms.\\nSee the Node.js documentation\\nfor details\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-javascript/v3/developer-guide/node-reusing-connections.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Programming Amazon DynamoDB with JavaScript\",\"context\":\"### Config for keep-alive\\n\\nWhen using HTTPS, the first request always takes some back-and-forth communication\\nto establish a secure connection. HTTP Keep-Alive allows subsequent requests to\\nreuse the already-established connection, making the requests more efficient and\\nlowering latency. HTTP Keep-Alive is enabled by default with JavaScript V3.\\n\\nThere's a limit to how long an idle connection can be kept alive. Consider sending\\nperiodic requests, maybe every minute, if you have an idle connection but want the\\nnext request to use an already-established connection.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nNote that in the older V2 of the SDK, keep-alive was off by default, meaning\\neach connection would get closed immediately after use. If using V2, you can\\noverride this setting\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/programming-with-javascript.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot 504 errors returned when I use a Classic Load Balancer?\",\"context\":\"### Make sure that your backend instances keep connections open\\n\\nWhen the backend instance closes a TCP connection to the load balancer before it reaches its idle timeout value, an HTTP 504 error might appear.\\n\\nTo resolve this issue, activate keep-alive settings on your backend instances. Then, set the keep-alive timeout to a value greater than the load balancer's idle timeout\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/504-error-classic\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs on keep-alive HTTP connection reuse best practices for AWS SDKs", "parent_id": "5d2402d4-792a-4d70-b750-2611de042b72"}

{"id": "4b83d22f-89c3-4b85-9710-259eef397aaa", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_aotIkSFvUim0Wqd22ksZUc", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Read Performance Considerations\",\"context\":\"# Read Performance Considerations\\n\\nWith the launch of\\nAmazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), you can now get microsecond\\naccess to data that lives in Amazon DynamoDB. DAX is an\\nin-memory cache in front of DynamoDB and has the identical API\\nas DynamoDB.\\n\\nBecause reads can be served from the DAX layer for queries with\\na cache hit, and the table will only serve the reads when there\\nis a cache miss, the provisioned read capacity units can be\\nlowered for cost savings.\\n\\n**Tip:** Based on the size of\\nyour tables and data access pattern, consider provisioning a\\nsingle DAX cluster for multiple smaller tables or multiple DAX\\nclusters for a single bigger table or a hybrid caching strategy\\nthat will work best for your application\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/comparing-dynamodb-and-hbase-for-nosql/read-performance-considerations.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Sizing your DAX cluster\",\"context\":\"## Planning read throughput\\n\\nA DAX cluster's read capacity depends on the cache hit ratio of your workload. Because DAX reads data from DynamoDB when a cache miss occurs, it consumes approximately 10 times more cluster resources than a cache-hit. To increase cache hits, increase the TTL setting of the cache to define the period for which an item is stored in the cache. A higher TTL duration, however, increases the chance of reading older item versions unless updates are written through DAX.\\n\\nTo make sure that the cluster has sufficient read capacity, scale the cluster horizontally as mentioned in Scaling a cluster horizontally. Adding more nodes adds read replicas to the pool of resources, while removing nodes reduces read capacity. When you select the number of nodes and their sizes for a cluster, consider both the minimum and maximum amount of read capacity needed. If you can't horizontally scale a cluster with smaller node types to meet your read requirements, use a larger node type\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/dax-cluster-sizing.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How can I troubleshoot high latency on DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters?\",\"context\":\"### Missed items in the cache\\n\\nIf a read request misses an item, then DAX sends the request to DynamoDB. DynamoDB processes the requests using eventually consistent reads and then returns the items to DAX. DAX stores them in the item cache and then returns them to the application. Latency in the underlying DynamoDB table can cause latency in the request.\\n\\nCache misses commonly happen for two reasons:\\n\\n1.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0**Strongly consistent reads:** Strongly consistent reads for the same item aren't cached by DAX. This results in a cache miss because the entries bypass DAX and are retrieved from the DynamoDB table itself. You can use eventually consistent reads to solve this issue, but note that DynamoDB must first read the data for the data to be cached.\\n\\n2.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0**Eviction policy in DAX:** Queried data that's already evicted from the cache results in a miss. DAX uses three different values to determine cache evictions:\\n\\n* DAX clusters use a Least Recently Used (LRU) algorithm to prioritize items. Items with the lowest priority are evicted when the cache is full.\\n* DAX uses a Time-to-Live (TTL) value for the period of time that items are available in the cache. After an item's TTL value is exceeded, the item is evicted. \\n**Note:** If you're using the default TTL value of five minutes, then check to see if you're querying the data after the TTL time.\\n* DAX uses [write-through functionality](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.consistency.html) to evict older values as new values are written. This helps keep the DAX item cache consistent with the underlying data store, using a single API call.\\n\\nTo extend the TTL value of your items, see [Configuring TTL settings](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.cluster-management.html#DAX.cluster-management.custom-settings.ttl). \\n**Note:** You can't modify a parameter group while it's in use in a running DAX instance.\\n\\nCache misses can also occur when maintenance patching is applied to a DAX cluster. Use multiple node clusters to reduce this downtime\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/high-latency-dax-clusters\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs on DynamoDB Scan operations with DAX caching behavior", "parent_id": "5d2402d4-792a-4d70-b750-2611de042b72"}

{"id": "8fc27b2e-727e-48a5-ab23-b77a45414d19", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_imGqK6sA8gCb7jXjAJCwHq", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Why doesn't my DynamoDB GetItem operation return the latest data even though PutItem is successful?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n----------\\n\\nDynamoDB tables and local secondary indexes (LSIs) provide two read consistency options: **eventually consistent** and **strongly consistent**. The read option is set to **eventually consistent** by default.\\n\\nThe\u00a0[GetItem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_GetItem.html) operation provides an eventually consistent read by default. An eventually consistent read might not be able to access data immediately after the data is written to the table. To get the latest data, wait for a short amount of time, then try your read request again.\\n\\nTo retrieve the latest data as soon as the write request completes, set the **ConsistentRead** parameter to **true**. This activates strongly consistent reads. Before you activate strongly consistent reads, consider the following:\\n\\n* Strongly consistent reads might have higher latency.\\n* Strongly consistent reads aren't supported on global secondary indexes.\\n* Strongly consistent reads require twice as much throughput as eventually consistent reads. This means that strongly consistent reads cost twice as expensive as eventually consistent reads. For more information, see [Pricing for provisioned capacity](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/provisioned/) and [Pricing for on-demand capacity](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/pricing/on-demand/).\\n\\nFor an example request that uses strongly consistent reads, see [Retrieve item attributes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_GetItem.html#API_GetItem_Example_1).\\n\\nRelated information\\n-------------------\\n\\n[PutItem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_PutItem.html) \\n \\n[Read consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/dynamodb-putitem-getitem-latest-data\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Evaluate your DynamoDB table usage patterns\",\"context\":\"## Perform fewer strongly-consistent read operations\\n\\nDynamoDB allows you to configure read\\nconsistency on a per-request basis. Read requests are eventually consistent by\\ndefault. Eventually consistent reads are charged at 0.5 RCU for upto 4 KB of data.\\n\\nMost parts of distributed workloads are flexible and can tolerate eventual consistency.\\nHowever, there can be access patterns requiring strongly consistent reads. Strongly consistent\\nreads are charged at 1 RCU for upto 4 KB of data, essentially doubling your read costs. DynamoDB\\nprovides you with the flexibility to use both consistency models on the same table.\\n\\nYou can evaluate your workload and application code to confirm if strongly consistent\\nreads are used only where required\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CostOptimization_TableUsagePatterns.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Class: Aws::DynamoDB::Types::ProvisionedThroughputDescription\\n \\n \u2014 AWS SDK for Ruby V3\",\"context\":\"### #**read_capacity_units** \u21d2 Integer\\n\\nThe maximum number of strongly consistent reads consumed per second\\nbefore DynamoDB returns a `ThrottlingException`. {"id": "5d2402d4-792a-4d70-b750-2611de042b72", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "run_subagent", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_vzeLHqLFLvvluGlqXYmevs", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "## Investigation Summary

**No DynamoDB-specific skill or remote runbook exists in this agent space.** I checked `list_associations` (only one association configured: a read-only AWS account monitor association — no wiki/Confluence/runbook association) and reviewed the skill catalog (skills cover pipelines, topology, metrics, traces, logs, Resilience Hub, etc. — none target DynamoDB/SDK latency specifically). So the evaluation below is grounded in **official AWS documentation and AWS knowledge-center guidance** (DynamoDB Developer Guide "Programming DynamoDB with JavaScript", AWS SDK for JS v3 Developer Guide "Reusing connections"/"Configuring maxSockets", and repost.aws troubleshooting articles on DynamoDB timeouts and DAX latency), not an internal runbook.

---

### 1. Set SDK socket timeout to 50ms
- **What guidance says:** AWS's own DynamoDB SDK docs explicitly warn: *"Don't set extremely low timeouts or you risk all requests failing during times of elevated latency."* In JS v3, the relevant `NodeHttpHandler` knobs are `connectionTimeout` (TCP/TLS establishment) and `requestTimeout` (time waiting for a response after the request is sent — this is what "socket timeout" maps to; some older docs/examples still label it `socketTimeout`). Both default to `0` (disabled/no limit) — they do **not** come pre-tuned, so the team is right that it's currently unbounded, but default DynamoDB socket/request timeout guidance elsewhere (Java SDK) is ~30s default with recommendation to only drop to 4–10s range.
- **Verdict: Anti-pattern.** 50ms is far below realistic DynamoDB round-trip times under any real-world network jitter, GC pause, or transient throttling — even healthy p50s can exceed this intermittently.
- **Risk/tradeoff:** This is a classic **retry-storm trigger**: a 50ms ceiling will time out a meaningful fraction of otherwise-successful requests, each of which gets retried (SDK v3 default retry behavior adds exponential backoff + jitter, up to several attempts for DynamoDB). Under load this amplifies request volume, consumes more capacity, increases queueing, and — ironically — **worsens p99** rather than bounding it, since timed-out+retried requests now show higher end-to-end latency than if they'd just been allowed to complete.
- **Better alternative:** Set `requestTimeout`/`connectionTimeout` to a realistic value (start at 1–3s for DynamoDB, not milliseconds) and tune based on measured p99.9 under normal load, not aspirational numbers. For genuine tail-latency reduction, AWS's own guidance points to **request hedging** (fire a second concurrent request if the first is slow past a threshold, take whichever returns first) — referenced directly in AWS's DynamoDB Java SDK docs via the "Global Payments Inc. improved their tail latency using request hedging with DynamoDB" blog — as the correct pattern for controlling tail latency, rather than aggressive timeouts.

### 2. Switch all reads to strongly consistent reads
- **What guidance says:** DynamoDB docs are explicit: strongly consistent reads (`ConsistentRead: true`) **consume twice the RCUs** of eventually consistent reads, **can have higher latency**, and **are not supported on GSIs**. AWS cost-optimization guidance recommends using strong consistency only where strictly required, not as a blanket default.
- **Verdict: Anti-pattern for a latency fix** — this is backwards. It does not address p99 tail latency; it's more likely to make it worse.
- **Risk/tradeoff:** Doubling RCU consumption raises the chance of throttling under provisioned capacity (directly increasing p99 due to retries), and if DAX is in play, strongly consistent reads **bypass the DAX cache entirely** (DAX passes them straight through to DynamoDB without caching the result) — so combining this with DAX (see item 3) actively defeats caching.
- **Better alternative:** Default to eventually consistent reads except for the specific access patterns that genuinely require read-your-own-write guarantees (e.g., immediately after a write in the same request flow). Isolate those cases rather than making it global.

### 3. Put DAX in front of a nightly Scan job
- **What guidance says:** AWS's DAX troubleshooting and sizing docs indicate DAX is designed for **high-read, repeated key-access patterns** with good cache-hit ratios; a cache miss costs roughly **10x** the cluster resources of a hit. `Scan` operations traverse the entire table and are inherently low-repeat/low-locality — a nightly batch Scan has essentially no "same item requested again" pattern for DAX's LRU/TTL cache to exploit, so it will be almost all cache misses.
- **Verdict: Anti-pattern / doesn't help.** DAX caches **individual items/query results**, not scan results in any useful way for a one-shot batch job; it adds cost and an extra network hop with no latency benefit, and can actually make things worse by driving the cluster to its cache-miss-amplified resource cost.
- **Risk/tradeoff:** Paying for a DAX cluster that never gets hit-rate benefit on this workload; a large Scan could also evict genuinely hot items from the cache (LRU eviction), degrading DAX's benefit for *other* latency-sensitive read traffic that legitimately benefits from it.
- **Better alternative:** Don't put DAX in front of Scan. For a nightly batch job, use **parallel Scan with segments**, or better, migrate to **on-demand export to S3 (DynamoDB Export to S3)** or **DynamoDB Streams** for batch/analytics use cases, which avoids consuming read capacity / impacting live traffic latency entirely. Reserve DAX for the actual low-latency point-lookup/query traffic that's causing the p99 complaint.

### 4. Add a keep-alive GetItem call every 30 seconds "to reuse connections"
- **What guidance says:** This is partially grounded in real AWS guidance but is a misapplication. AWS's SDK v3 docs confirm: (a) **TCP connection reuse (keep-alive) is already enabled by default** in SDK v3's `NodeHttpHandler` — the team doesn't need to do anything to get baseline connection reuse; (b) AWS docs *do* suggest sending periodic "ping" requests roughly every minute specifically to keep an **idle** connection warm so the *next real* request doesn't pay TCP/TLS handshake cost — but that's a mitigation for idle/bursty traffic patterns, not for a service with steady request volume.
- **Verdict: Partially right idea, poorly targeted — not the actual fix for p99 under load.** It only keeps **one** connection in the agent's pool warm. SDK v3's `NodeHttpHandler` uses a connection pool (`maxSockets`, default commonly 50) — under real concurrency, many parallel requests use many sockets simultaneously, and a single keep-alive ping does nothing to pre-warm the rest of the pool or to prevent new-connection cost when concurrency spikes above however many sockets are already open.
- **Risk/tradeoff:** Extra GetItem calls cost RCU and add noise/cost for negligible benefit if traffic is already steady (keep-alive is already default). It gives a false sense of having "solved" connection overhead while the real tail-latency driver is more likely to be connection-pool sizing (`maxSockets`) under concurrency, DNS/TLS session reuse, or Nagle/delayed-ACK effects — none of which a single periodic GetItem touches.
- **Better alternative:** Verify `keepAlive` is true (it is, by default) and tune `maxSockets` upward if sustained concurrency regularly approaches/exceeds the default limit (AWS explicitly calls out considering this when concurrency is ~50+) — that directly reduces new-connection-establishment latency under load, which the keep-alive-ping idea does not. Only use a periodic keep-alive ping for genuinely idle/bursty clients (e.g., a connection that goes quiet for minutes between calls), not as a general p99 remedy for an active service.

### On the SDK v3 config knobs themselves
The team's assumptions about *what knobs exist* are roughly correct but imprecise: JS v3 `NodeHttpHandler` exposes `connectionTimeout` and `requestTimeout` (not a literal `socketTimeout` property in current official docs, though it's sometimes referenced/aliased that way in older examples) — so "socket timeout" should be understood as `requestTimeout`. Keep-alive/connection reuse is controlled via `httpsAgent`/`httpAgent` (Node `Agent` with `keepAlive`, `keepAliveMsecs`) and `maxSockets`, all defaulted sensibly already (keep-alive on by default in v3, unlike v2). Retries are governed separately by `maxAttempts`/retry strategy, which interacts dangerously with item 1's aggressive timeout.

---

**Suggested deeper follow-ups** (shallow research performed; happy to go deeper):
- Pull actual CloudWatch DynamoDB `SuccessfulRequestLatency` p50/p90/p99 and `ThrottledRequests`/`ConsumedReadCapacityUnits` for the real tables to see if current latency is throttling-driven (favoring capacity/partition-key fixes) vs. connection-layer (favoring `maxSockets`/hedging).
- Check actual `NodeHttpHandler`/`Agent` config in the service's code (via `exploring-code` skill) to confirm current `maxSockets`, `keepAlive`, and timeout values rather than assumed defaults.
- If hedging is adopted, review the Global Payments/AWS Database Blog case study in detail for implementation pattern and guardrails (e.g., hedge-request cancellation, capacity cost of duplicate requests)."}]}], "label": "Look up DynamoDB latency guidance to evaluate four proposed SDK/DynamoDB changes."}

Here's the verdict on each item — three of the four are anti-patterns that would likely make p99 worse, not better.

**1. 50ms socket timeout — Anti-pattern, likely to backfire**
This is a textbook retry-storm trigger. 50ms is below realistic DynamoDB round-trip times even when healthy; AWS's own docs warn against extremely low timeouts because they cause "all requests failing during times of elevated latency." Timed-out requests get retried by the SDK's default retry strategy, which adds *more* load and *more* latency — the opposite of the goal.
- Fix instead: tune `requestTimeout`/`connectionTimeout` (JS v3's actual knobs — there's no literal `socketTimeout` property) to something like 1–3s based on measured p99.9, not an aspirational number. For real tail-latency control, AWS documents **request hedging** (fire a second concurrent request if the first is slow, take whichever returns first) as the correct pattern — not aggressive timeouts.

**2. Strongly consistent reads everywhere — Backwards fix**
Strongly consistent reads consume **2x the RCUs**, can have *higher* latency, and aren't supported on GSIs. Doubling capacity consumption raises throttling risk, which directly hurts p99. Worse, it conflicts with item 3/DAX: strongly consistent reads bypass the DAX cache entirely.
- Fix instead: default to eventually consistent reads; reserve strong consistency only for the specific read-your-own-write cases that need it.

**3. DAX in front of the nightly Scan job — Doesn't help**
DAX earns its value on repeated point-lookups/queries with good cache-hit ratios (a miss costs ~10x a hit). A one-shot nightly `Scan` has no "same item again" locality — it's nearly all cache misses, and it can evict genuinely hot items from the cache via LRU, hurting *other* latency-sensitive traffic.
- Fix instead: use parallel Scan with segments, or move batch/analytics reads off the live read path entirely (DynamoDB Export to S3, or Streams). Save DAX for the actual point-lookup traffic driving the p99 complaint.

**4. Keep-alive GetItem every 30s — Right instinct, wrong target**
Partially grounded in real guidance, but misapplied. SDK v3 already enables keep-alive/connection reuse **by default** — no action needed there. A periodic ping only keeps *one* pooled connection warm; under real concurrency the pool uses many sockets (`maxSockets`, default ~50), so this does nothing for the rest of the pool and doesn't prevent new-connection cost when concurrency spikes.
- Fix instead: confirm `keepAlive` is on (it is by default) and raise `maxSockets` if sustained concurrency approaches the default limit — that's what actually reduces connection-establishment latency under load. Keep-alive pings are for genuinely idle/bursty clients, not steady traffic.

**Bottom line:** none of these four directly diagnoses *why* p99 is bad — they're reaching for mechanism changes without a root cause. The highest-leverage next step is pulling actual `SuccessfulRequestLatency` p50/p90/p99 and throttling metrics for the real tables to see whether this is capacity/throttling-driven or connection-layer-driven, since that determines whether hedging, `maxSockets` tuning, or partition-key/capacity fixes are the right lever.
